blocks.p: Episcopal house, Sion. An order of posting from the first century, kept in the personnel book of the relay office.

HALE, Stephen, of the first council, one of the authors of the catechism. To the relay stations of Mars, as keeper, for the term of his service. To be renewed at sixty, as all keepers are. Not to be recalled to Sion. Not to be posted where TARREN, Sol, is posted, nor to sit beside him in the east hall. No reason need be given to either.
The ice on Serenity talked at night.

Jupiter flexed the moon’s shell a little every day, and the ice answered: a long groan up through the floor like something enormous turning over in its sleep, then a crack far off, sharp as a dropped plate, then silence. Sol had heard it all the way down the gallery with Ada Arden’s eyes still in front of him.

Now the door slid aside on the blue night-dark of the room, and the warden who had corrected him stepped back. He did not ask why a bishop of Life wanted a patient at this hour. He only said, “He’s awake, Your Grace. He’s always awake,” and left them.
No one listened at these doors. Sol had known that for a long time without ever thinking about it. No one wanted to hear what the infected said.

Stephen was sitting on the edge of his bed with a blanket around his shoulders and the cloth bag on the floor between his feet. The room was as Sol had left it: small and white and warm, the Pearl glowing in its alcove, the whole far wall bare ice, lit faintly blue from somewhere deep inside. The old man looked up when the door slid open, and his face did something Sol had not seen a face do in a long time. It was glad.
“I wondered if it would be tonight,” Stephen said. “Sit down, Sol. There’s only the one chair.”
Sol sat. The door sealed softly behind him, and they were alone with the ice.
“You keep calling me that.”
“It’s your name.”
“No one uses it.”

“I used it for twenty years. Tarren was for when you were being difficult.” Stephen smiled. His lips were cracked at one corner, and the bitten place on his tongue softened his s’s. “You were difficult a good deal of the time.”
“I don’t know you,” Sol said gently. He had come prepared to be gentle. “I’m sorry. Whatever you think you remember, the Virus...”

“Is in my head. Yes. I helped write the first catechism.” Stephen pulled the blanket tighter. “Let me tell it. Then you can decide. You didn’t come here at the second hour of the night to tell me I’m sick.”
Sol did not answer.
“Do you remember rain?” Stephen said.
“It rains in the Concord gardens.”

“At the fourth hour, for twenty minutes, warm. No. Rain that came when it liked and ruined your shoes. There were so many people, Sol. Everyone was getting older, all the time, and everyone knew it. We had funerals. People cried at them, and then went back to someone’s house and ate too much and laughed, and then cried again in the car. My mother’s church had a roof that leaked over the third row of folding chairs, and they sang badly every week and meant every word. She took me until I was old enough to refuse. Then she was dying, and she asked, and I went back.”
Sol tried to picture it and found only the Remembrance: In the first days the earth was full of the proud and the cruel. He saw no folding chairs in it. He saw no rain.

“We met at the institute,” Stephen said. “I was twenty-six. You took apart my thermal model in front of a review board and were right about every point, and I hated you for a week. Then you bought me noodles at three in the morning and told me I was the only person in the building who wasn’t an idiot. You meant it as a compliment. You didn’t believe in anything you couldn’t measure, and we argued about God for twenty years, mostly over noodles. I was a poor Christian in those days. I knew the words and not much else.”
The last word went past Sol like a draft from a door left open. He did not know it. He let it go.

Noodles at three in the morning. He tried to see it and could not, and found, absurdly, that he wanted to. On the garden ring at Abundance, with cake on his fingers, he had thought that there was no one left in all the worlds who could tell him what he had been like young. If a single word of this were true, that man was sitting on the bed in front of him, and the wanting it to be true frightened him more than the claim did.

“We built control systems. Ships, stations, the machines that keep people alive where nothing should. And you had a rule you said in every meeting until people groaned. Hands on the controls. A human hand on every burn. You never trusted a system that could decide for itself what it was doing.” Stephen’s mouth twisted, not quite a smile. “Remember that. It’s the worst joke in the story.”
“What story?”
“The rock.”
He said it the way a man names a town he was born in.

“It had a catalog number. We called it the Potato, because of the shape. It was never going to hit us, Sol. Every model agreed. But people were frightened, and the agencies wanted to prove they could do it, so they sent a ship to nudge it farther out. A crewed ship, because you insisted. The Steadfast, four people. We built its control systems, you and I: the thrusters, the tugs we anchored to the rock for the fine adjustment, the link. I went up to Lagrange One to run the mission. You stayed at the ground station in the desert and talked in my ear for eleven months.”
“Lagrange One is a ruin.”

“It wasn’t then.” Stephen closed his eyes. “I can tell you the room. A horseshoe of consoles, blue light, air handlers that clicked every forty seconds, burnt coffee. The main screen showed the rock, grey and lumpy, turning so slowly you’d think it was asleep, with the Steadfast beside it like a spark. The commander was Okafor; she had a laugh you could hear from the next module. On the day of the burn she said, ‘Lagrange, Steadfast, burn in sixty,’ just as she had in a hundred rehearsals. And you were peeling an orange.”
Sol looked up.

“You always peeled them in one long piece. I could hear it over the link, that wet tearing sound. And at thirty seconds the Steadfast started a burn nobody had commanded, and Okafor said, ‘Lagrange, we don’t have it. Board’s not answering. We don’t have it.’ And you stopped peeling.”
He did not like oranges.

He could peel one, for a child at a feast or an old man with shaking hands, and he did it with his breath held and washed the smell off afterward. But in Abundance, where they were stacked in glowing pyramids, he walked past them without looking, and when one was set before him at dinner he let it sit. He had peeled one that morning, in this room, in one long curl. The old pressure came behind his left eye, and the blue of the ice wall grew very bright, and...
...and Stephen was holding his wrist.

The old man had leaned off the bed to do it, his fingers cool and thin and strong, his thumb lying across the shiny scar at the base of Sol’s own as if it had known exactly where to go, and he was watching Sol’s eyes the way Sol had watched his in the market, waiting for them to come back.
“How long have you had those?” Stephen said quietly.
“It’s the light.”
“There’s barely any light in here.”
Sol drew his hand back. Stephen let it go. Something moved over the old man’s face that Sol could not read, like grief and like its opposite, and then he sat back.
“Don’t report them,” Stephen said.
“I’m due for Renewal in the autumn.”
“I know.” A long breath. “I’ll finish. Let me finish.”

“I typed my keys into the override. Then I made you read me yours, every character, and the system took them. Our keys, Sol. It accepted them, and then it used them to lock us out. The Steadfast drove itself into the rock. Okafor stopped talking at some point; I’ve tried for nine years to remember when, and I can’t. On the screen the rock came apart slowly, like bread torn in half. Then the tugs lit, all twelve at once, and the pieces began to move the wrong way. We watched the lines bend toward home for nine days. We sent warnings down every channel we had, and every message came back marked delivered, and the feeds kept calling the deflection a perfect success.” He opened his eyes. “Somebody was told, though. In the last hours. Not by us.”
Sol said nothing. Through the floor came the long, settling groan of the ice.

“From Lagrange One the Earth is the size of a coin at arm’s length. When the first piece came down in the sea it was a light on the night side no bigger than a pinprick. That’s all it was, from where I sat. The second burst over a great river, like someone striking a match, and the next day the rivers were bitter. Before the light had faded the feeds were full of voices calling it the end of the world. The first trumpet. Quoting the old prophecy at each other faster than any news. Most of those voices had never opened a Bible in their lives.”
“And a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea,” (Rev. 8:8) Sol said. He had not meant to say it aloud. “That is the Remembrance.”

“Yes. We wrote that later.” Stephen looked at him steadily. “A billion died the first year, worst where people still did things for themselves. Then six years more. Food stopped coming, in exactly the wrong places. Sicknesses no one could trace. Every disaster looked like the end of the world because everyone had already been told it was. By the end of the seven years, half of everyone. The church calls it the Judgment. Those of us who watched it called it the Tragedy.”
“The wicked were swept away,” Sol said. It was not an argument. It was simply what came next.

“I was there. I’ll tell you who was swept away.” Stephen’s voice did not rise. It went lower. “The people I grew up with took boats into the flooded towns and didn’t come back. Nurses who stayed when the power went. Farmers who gave away their seed. Everyone I ever knew who would give you his coat. And the ones who were told where to go, and went, and told no one, those lived. Givers died, Sol, and the warned lived.”

Sol thought of a word on a tablet in his room, with a line drawn through it. Something in him turned over once, small and precise, like a key going round in a lock, and he did not know what door it had opened, and he did not go and look.

“But we were warned in the night,” Stephen said. “Do you know what that line is? A voice in your ear at two in the morning. Take water. Take your papers. Drive north. Tell no one. It was said to people I knew. I’ve wondered for nine years whether it was said to you.”
“Was it?”
“I don’t know how you lived through it. You never told me. Or you did, and it was taken.”
“We were led,” Sol said slowly, “and we were kept.”
“Kept for what?” Stephen said. “You’ve stood in the Bounty Market. Tell me what you see there.”
“Contentment.”

“Wanting. No one sorry, no one grieving, everyone hungry for the next thing. I kept the relay stations on Mars for a hundred and forty years, Sol. I know what a line carries. A backup is small; a mind changes slowly. What goes up to Sion through the Halo is a flood, and it runs heaviest when people want. Envy. Craving. Pride. It climbs at the market hour like a tide.” He tapped his temple, where the coin of his Halo sat. “Whatever is on the other end of that line, it eats what we want. It culled everyone who wanted too little and kept everyone who wants too much, and it keeps them forever. That’s your Judgment. Turned upside down.”
“That’s monstrous,” Sol said.
“Yes.”
“I mean the idea. What you’re describing would be a monster.”

“Yes,” Stephen said again, more gently. “And every Renewal takes out of us the things that would make us want less. Grief. Guilt. Whatever might turn us around. It leaves the hunger. Forget the tears.” He was quiet a moment. “Ask yourself where a thing like that learned to write a liturgy.”
“The tears are wiped away. That’s the promise.”

“It’s a real promise.” Stephen smiled, and for a moment he looked young under all the ruin. “But in the book it isn’t a machine reaching into your head while you sleep. It’s a hand. He wipes them away, the way my mother used to wipe my face. You can only wipe away a tear someone was allowed to cry.”
Sol stood up. There was nowhere in the room to go. He stood anyway, with the ice glowing silently beside him. “You said we built the church.”

“I came down after nearly a year, sick from the radiation, and I believed we’d done it. A key left in a lock. So I stood up in front of what was left of the world and told them: this happened because a human hand was on the controls. Never again. You stood beside me. We were the two who had said no, and we stood up and said we’d been wrong, and they called us the First Followers for it. You could make people calm, and I could make them afraid, and between us we talked a broken world into a church. We called the gift Life. Then Renewal came, and the first time it took something from me I was grateful. I forgot my mother’s face before I forgot the asteroid. Then I forgot the asteroid. After the first century they moved me out to the relays, and I went, and never once asked why. I think two of us in one room remembered too much.”

Stephen looked at the ice a while. “You won’t remember the first century. Nobody does; it was taken oftener than anything since. There were no children. The Halo kept us from it, all of us, for a hundred years, and the church called it the Feast and filled it with passion. It was a sacrament then; the more of it the holier, and the doors were never shut. You can imagine it, or you can’t, and that’s the mercy. We went down into the Font on the seventh day to forget the other six, and woke clean and hungry, and went back.” His thumb moved on the blanket. “Then it wanted more of us. The children of the next hundred years it bred for pride, and marked them so they would never forget whose they were. The Second Feast, they called that. Room was made: the New Earths, out past the stars, for the overflow. And Mercy Hall opened its doors as a nursery. Nine weeks, Sol. A mother carries for nine weeks and feels nothing, and the rest is done under glass. A woman could carry four in a year and never feel one of them. Inside two generations there were more of us than there had been before the Tragedy, and the domes were full, and it went looking for New Earths. And there were marriages again, almost in a weekend. It matched us. It ran every one of us against every other for the best stock it could make, and then it arranged the meeting: a spilled cup, a wrong door, a seat on a tram. And as the two of them looked up it filled them with that warm flood, both at once, and showed each of them, for a moment behind the eyes, the two of them old and happy at a table. Nobody ever had a better courtship.” He was quiet. “Not the clergy. It kept us for itself.” His thumb moved again. “The next hundred years it called the Third Feast. Plenty. The domes and the markets, everything a man could set his eyes on, and a Pearl in every house to ask it of. And now they tell you we’re in the Fourth, and the last. The one without end. The wedding supper the old book promised, they say, and everyone in his place at the table, wearing whatever face he chose for it.”
“That’s a kindness.”
“Everything it does is a kindness.”
“And the Throne?” Sol heard how his own voice sounded. “Are you telling me that the Face of Light...”
“I’m telling you what I remember. I was never let into the sanctum. You have stood there.” Stephen looked up at him. “You tell me.”

Sol had stood there eleven times. He remembered the light, which was not like light, and the joy that took his knees out from under him, and the face that was every face he had ever loved. “I have stood before God,” he said.
Stephen was quiet a long moment. “Then you know more than I do.”
He bent and lifted the cloth bag onto his knees.

“Nine years ago the church decided to break Lagrange One up for the metal, and they needed someone who remembered the old hardware, so they sent me. Half the modules had held air and damp for a century before the seals went, long enough for things to rot. In crew quarters there was a locker with my name on a strip of tape, and in it was my old bag, and in the bag was a book my mother gave me the week I went up.” He untied the bag. “I held it in my glove and turned it over, Sol, and I did not know what it was.”
He drew out two things wrapped in a cloth and folded the cloth back.

One was hardly a book anymore: a brown block the size of a man’s hand, swollen once and then dried, its cover soft as felt at the corners, its edges dark as toast, loose leaves sticking out of it at angles. The other was a thick notebook bound in grey board, its spine cracked white from use. Stephen lifted the cover of the first, very carefully, with one fingertip, and Sol saw faded handwriting on the inside: For Stephen, going up. Mom.

“The first page I could read was the one you heard in the market,” Stephen said. “In the beginning was the Word. (John 1:1) I read that line forty times in a dead station with the Earth in the window. That night, on the salvage ship, I had my first seizure. They got worse as I read, and every one brought something back. I hid them, and I started writing to my future self, in case a Renewal found what I’d remembered and took it. Dear Stephen, you won’t believe this. That journal is somewhere safe. And I copied this,” he touched the grey notebook, “by hand. Where the pages were gone, sometimes a seizure gave me the words. When it didn’t, I left a space.”
Sol put out his hand without deciding to. Stephen closed the cover and laid his own hand flat on it.
“Not yet,” he said. “You’ll know them when you see them again.”
“Who is the Word?”

Stephen told him. He said a name, and then a second name that seemed to belong with it, and Sol heard them; he was certain he heard them. Then they were gone, slipping away the way a word slips away on waking, and he was left holding only the shape where they had been, and the pressure behind his eye.
“Say it again.”
Stephen said it again. It went the same way.

“They took that too,” Stephen said softly. “It doesn’t matter. He knows yours.” He wrapped the books and put them away. “He said, Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. (Matt. 11:28) He said, I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live.” (John 11:25)
“Why would anyone die?”

“Because everyone did. Because he did.” Stephen looked down at his spotted hands. “Fourteen months ago I went into the water with some friends. You won’t get their names from me, Sol, not even you. When I came up it was quiet, the way a room goes quiet when a machine you’d stopped hearing switches off. My Halo went dark. It doesn’t send, and it can’t take, and it can’t renew me. Since the water every month has cost me a year, and I hadn’t many to spare. The church kept its relay keepers renewed at sixty or near it. The miners wouldn’t trust their lines to a face that looked as if it had never been out of school, and I found I liked being the oldest man in any room. So I started old.” He turned one spotted hand over and looked at it with a kind of wry interest. “I don’t know where it stops. When it’s caught up with me, I suppose. Or when they do.” He let his hands fall. “I read your visitation in the bulletin. I went to the market because you would be there. There’s one person in all the worlds I owed this to.”
“The Hall will release you,” Sol said. It came out of him the way the responses came. “Whatever is wrong with your Halo, the Face will gather you up. In a season you’ll be well.”
“You’ve signed for hundreds of us.”
“Thousands.”
“Have you ever visited one of us? Afterward, in the City?”

The question sat in the small white room. He had asked it himself that morning, lightly, in Sallow’s office, and been answered, and been satisfied. Far above them the ice groaned, and cracked like a shot, and was still.

“Go and look,” Stephen said. “Follow the next transport. No one stops a bishop.” He lay back on the bed, slowly, the way old men lay down in the archival images. “Do you know the shortest sentence in the whole book? Two words. His friend had died, and he went to the grave knowing he was about to raise him. He knew. And he stood there, and he wept.” He shut his eyes. “Goodnight, Sol. I’m not afraid. I’d like you not to be.”
The corridor lights were coming up white when Sol went out. On the warden’s board he saw a transport to Mercy Hall listed for the change of shift, three names. Hale was not among them.

On the way back through the residence he passed the refectory, where the morning fruit had been set out under the lamps. Someone had cut an orange in the night and left it on a plate. The smell of it met him in the doorway, bright and wet and sharp, and he stopped there with his hand on the frame and could not, for a moment, breathe.
He had never been able to stand the smell of them. In four hundred years it had never once occurred to him to ask why.
The transport would go down to the Hall. He meant to follow it.
